newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION - SAFRICA'S FISCAL SITUATION - BY E.OSBORN.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - SAFRICA'S FISCAL SITUATION - BY E.OSBORN.

text.p: By Edward Osborn, Economic Consultant to Edey, Rogers & Co. Ltd.
The nine-months fiscal situation for 1996/97 as revealed in the Exchequer Account returns for April-December would appear to be satisfactory.

Favourable publicity has already been given to the cumulative receipts and issues to date, which would be not inconsistent with the realisation of the expected budgetary deficit before borrowing of 5.1 percent of GDP.
But not acknowledged so far is the much improved discipline and control on the funding side.

Despite the reported tardiness with regard to RDP expenditures, total disbursements or, more accurately, issues to departments from exchequer, are running some three billion rand ahead of departmental projections.

This is clearly a pointer to substantial additional appropriations required in the February supplementary budget, but part of the problem is that the interest bill is turning out to be substantially higher than projected initially because it was first estimated on very sanguine assumptions.
This is graphically demonstrated by the actual discount on RSA stocks for the nine months of 5.7 billion rand, as compared with the projected discount of 2.8 billion rand for the full year.

Interest payments to date are 17.2 percent ahead of the comparable period last year and, assuming a repeat of the pattern of payments, can be projected to end the year at 34.4 billion rand, which would be an additional 850 million rand on budget.

Total non-interest expenditures are also running well above the budgeted rate (14.3 percent as against 8.6 percent), which is indicative of considerable spending pressures that will have to be addressed in the Additional Appropriation Budget.
No doubt much of this is coming from the provincial governments.
The interesting thing about spending, though, is that the so-called roll-overs have not turned out to be serious problems whatsoever.

Late departmental requisitions from the votes of previous years have only amounted to 370 million rand in the nine months and, indeed, this has been completely swamped by the surrenders of issues from previous years of 3.4 billion rand. The spectre of a 12 billion rand overhang has come to nought.

Revenue receipts into exchequer have been exceptionally buoyant with 74.7 percent of the budgeted 144.9 billion rand having been received in the nine months, as compared with 72.7 percent of the budgeted 127.3 billion rand for the same period in 1995.

Put another way receipts have grown by 17.96 percent in contrast to the budgeted growth of 13.8 percent. The analysis of revenue shows that the increase is primarily due to much-higher-than-projected income tax receipts but the depreciated rand has also played its part in boosting receipts from customs duties.
The Receiver of Revenue has delivered on his promises to lift revenues through improvements in collections and the collection of arrear taxes.
VAT revenues, however, have been disappointing, running at 11.3 percent above last year, as compared with budgetary expectations of 13.3 percent.

As a result of these buoyant revenues the deficit position to date is only R18.0 billion, identical to the comparable deficit last year. On this performance it is feasible that the actual deficit for the year will be no worse than the budgeted 28.8 billion rand, or 5.1 percent of GDP.
So extra revenues have fortuitously offset the inevitable departmental demands for higher expenditures.
But what has been praiseworthy has been the apparent better management of the funding operations of government this year.
Funding has been more constrained and restricted to the actual needs of the exchequer.

Last year there was a tendency to fund ahead of requirements, despite the protestations of the Minister of Finance at the time that funding would be more even and, therefore, less costly to the exchequer.

Taking account of much higher stock redemptions this year and other miscellaneous below-the-line transactions the net funding requirement in the nine months was 31.7 billion rand, as compared with 26.7 billion rand last year, despite the identical deficits before borrowing.

The total financing raised on a cash flow basis to date was 33.9 billion rand, giving a surplus of 2.2 billion rand. Last year 33.1 billion rand was raised through to December 1995, indicating a financing excess of as much as 6.6 billion rand.
The result of this improved management was a containment of the rise in government's balances in the Exchequer Account and the Tax and Loan accounts held with the commercial banks.
Total balances at the end of December 1996 amounted to 6.6 billion rand, as compared with 11.1 billion rand a year earlier.
The irony of the financing operations in 1996/96 was that the bulk of the funding operations in the local bond market was carried out when rates were high, although falling.
Cash balances were accumulated to a peak of 17.4 billion rand in January 1996 and then run down dramatically to 3.3 billion rand by the end of the fiscal year, March 1996.
In that last quarter there were very limited funding operations in the bond market when rates had dropped notably.
In short the funding operations of 1995/96 were totally out of phase with the bond market yields and proved to be costly to government.
In this 1996/97 year bond rates have been consistently higher in a 15 percent to 16.5 percent range and Treasury has tapped the market on a restrained basis according to need.
There were, of course, movements in residual balances from month-to-month but not inordinately.

Given the relatively modest level of balances in December and that there will be a net deficit accrual of another ten billion rand, government will have to maintain its funding operations in the local bond market at about ten billion rand in this first quarter of 1997.

Redemptions are insignificant in the quarter so that there is no additional funding required for them. Balances of the order of six billion rand have to be maintained for the regular transfers of monies to the provinces in the first few days of each month.

However, there is another aspect which has to be taken into account in explaining Treasury's move from extravagance to restraint in its funding behaving and that is the situation in the country at various stages regarding the overall level of liquidity.
There was a marked difference in the liquidity situation during 1995 and 1996.
In 1995 it was characterised by excess liquidity with the Reserve Bank having problems of mopping up liquidity.
The reverse situation developed in 1996 with persistent shortages in the money market, basically because of a reversal in the capital account of the balance of payments.

Accordingly Treasury's funding operations had to be used as a means of mopping up liquidity in 1995, whereas there was no longer any need for this in 1996 and, indeed, it had to go into the market to get only what it required.
On this reckoning we have to withdraw a few Brownie points from Treasury.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
24 January 1997
